div.head: Abt 61
div.ab: Gif hrifwund weorðeþ, XII scill' gebete.
Gif hrifwund weorðeþ, XII scill' gebete.
Gif hrif wund weorðeþ, XII sciƚƚ gebete.
Wenn [jener] im Bauch verwundet wird, büsse er 12 Schill.
If [that man] is wounded in the belly, let him pay 12 shillings.
If the belly is wounded, 12 shillings shall be paid as compensation.
If an abdominal wound occurs, let him pay [with] 12 shillings.

note.seg: Ellipse wie 7¹. 54¹; hrif (vgl. Gl Bauch) darf nicht von wund getrennt werden, weil 61, 1 he ‘[Verletzt]er’ fortfährt; das Adj. steht auch in Lex Alam. 57, 55
Ellipsis as at 7¹. 54¹; hrif (cf. Gl Bauch) must not be separated from wund, because 61, 1 continues with he ‘the [injur]ed man’; the adjective also occurs in Lex Alam. 57, 55
Dieselbe Busssumme auch Pact. Alam. 11; Lex Baiuwar. I 5, 5; Brunner II 636
The same amount of compensation is also found in Pact. Alam. 11; Lex Baiuwar. I 5, 5; Brunner II 636

note.label: wund
note.seg: Either hrif is the subject of the verb with wund serving as predicate, or the two form a compound subject; see parallel §68 and note a to translation.

note.label: shillings.
note.seg: This could also be translated: ‘If an abdomen becomes wounded …’ Indeed, hrif occurs only rarely as the first element of a compound in Old English. But the Lex Alamannorum (written sometime between 584 and 629) has hreuouunt (hreuo ~ hrif + wunt ~ wund), which also served as the model for hreuauunt in Lex Bavariorum (see Georg Baesecke, ‘Die deutschen Worte der germanischen Gesetze,’ Beiträge zur Geschichte der Deutschen Sprache und Literatur 59 [1935]: 1–101 at 19). Comparative evidence would thus suggest interpreting the Old English similarly as a compound.
